children: Suraksha P Bengaluru: Ability to provide reliable power supply at scale, create capacity faster and offer globally competitive electricity tariffs will matter more than fiscal incentives in determining which Indian states can emerge as major data centre hubs, industry executives told ET. As states roll out the red carpet to attract private investments in artificial intelligence (AI) and cloud infrastructure, delivering uninterrupted power to project sites from day one would be crucial for their success, they said. "Important thing is that we do not need any incentives from the state. What we need from the state is power," said Piyush Somani, chairman and managing director of ESDS Software Solution. Announcements of large investments and memoranda of understanding (MoUs) would remain on paper unless states could demonstrate the availability of power, Somani said.

Citing the example of a state that has announced policies and signed MoUs involving 5-6 GW of proposed data centre capacity, he said the question is whether it currently had even 500 MW of power available for such projects. Balaji Rajagopal, chief operating officer and principal advisor at Datasamudra, said the emphasis of Karnataka's data centre policy on sustainability, for example, while useful, will not be sufficient on its own. The immediate bottleneck for hyperscale and AI workloads is whether the state can deliver uninterrupted, high quality power at scale, with substations and transmission infrastructure ready in the right locations, he said. "The policy is a good start, but it cannot substitute for a broader ecosystem push that includes grid upgrades, land readiness and long-term cost competitiveness," Rajagopal said.

Several states, from Maharashtra, Uttar Pradesh, Gujarat, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Telangana and Andhra Pradesh to Odisha, Bihar, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, Manipur, Rajasthan, Tripura and West Bengal, have announced dedicated data centre policies to attract digital and AI infrastructure investments.

Karnataka policy On September 18, Karnataka approved its Sustainable Data Centre Policy 2026-31 with a budget of about 1,300.45 crore. The policy targets 1 GW of cumulative IT load by 2031. A broader ecosystem push, including grid upgrades, land readiness, subsea fibre connectivity and long-term cost competitiveness, will be key for attracting investments, executives said while welcoming incentives for water and power efficiency. "Infrastructure must precede incentives.

You cannot put the policy cart before the utility horse," Neil Shah, cofounder and vice president for research at Counterpoint Research, said. "Multi-billion-dollar AI infrastructure rollouts depend primarily on ready, reliable power, which directly dictates AI tokenomics," he said.

Fiscal concessions barely scratch the surface." This is visible in investment flows. Navi Mumbai and Chennai have emerged as leading locations because they had built dedicated transmission headroom and high voltage substations before demand peaked, while also benefiting from active coastal subsea cable landings, he said. "Even inland hubs like Hyderabad gained early traction only because they fast-tracked dedicated 220-400 kV substations in campuses like Chandanvelly," Shah said. "In contrast, emerging hubs like Vizag have seen ambitious MoUs stall simply because local grids cannot energise even 200-500 MW on schedule." Suyog Keluskar, senior director, industrial goods and services, at market intelligence firm 1Lattice, said the key constraint for data centre expansion was no longer generation capacity as the national deficit is near zero. "What decides where data centres land is how fast firm power reaches a specific site - a sequencing question, not an incentive question," he said.
